entries.topic: The names Ashkenaz, Sepharad and Mizrahi: biblical geography and modern usage

claims.text: Ashkenaz appears in Genesis 10:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:6 as a descendant of Gomer, and in Jeremiah 51:27 as a kingdom called to rise against Babylon. In medieval rabbinic literature the name was used for Germany.

Sepharad appears in Obadiah (v. 20) as a place where exiles from Jerusalem lived; its original location is unknown. The Aramaic Targum Jonathan is the earliest known source to render it as Spain ('Ispamia'), and by the 9th century the name denoted the Iberian Peninsula in Jewish usage.

'Sephardi' and 'Ashkenazi' are also used for liturgical rites: 'Sephardim' can mean Jews who follow the Spanish rite and 'Ashkenazim' those who follow the German rite, whatever their family origin. Israeli official usage and the Chief Rabbinate place many Mizrahi communities under the 'Sephardi' heading.

My Jewish Learning describes 'Mizrahi' as a socio-political term for Jews from Arab and/or Muslim lands, coined by Israel's Ashkenazi establishment in the 1950s and later adopted by many immigrants for themselves.

Other scholarship dates the category earlier: Gil Eyal (2006) places its invention in the Jewish Agency's 1940s 'One Million Plan', and demographer Roberto Bachi used 'Mizrahim' and 'Ashkenazim' as categories for the Yishuv in the 1940s. Sources therefore disagree on whether the umbrella term dates from the 1940s or the 1950s.

Before 1948 many of these communities did not see themselves as one group and often called themselves Sephardim. Writers including Ella Shohat (1999) and novelist Sami Michael have criticised the umbrella term as a construction, and many people still prefer to name their country of origin.

North African Jews were historically called 'Westerners' (Maghribiyyun) rather than 'Easterners', and including them under 'Mizrahi' is contested; the Wikipedia statement that many object to this lacks a citation.

entries.topic: Ashkenazi Jews: Rhineland origins, Poland–Lithuania, Yiddish

claims.text: By the 10th century there were centres of rabbinic learning at Mainz and Worms in the Rhineland and at Troyes and Sens in France; in the Middle Ages the name Ashkenaz was applied to the Jews living along the Rhine.

Britannica describes the Ashkenazim as Jews of the Rhineland and neighbouring France who migrated eastward to Slavic lands (Poland, Lithuania, Russia) after the Crusades of the 11th to 13th centuries.

Citing the historian Bernard Weinryb, EGO treats the 13th and especially 14th centuries as the period of real Jewish settlement in Poland. It followed royal charters from Bolesław in 1264 and Casimir the Great in 1334, and privileges granted by Grand Duke Vytautas in Lithuania in 1388.

The Encyclopaedia Judaica-based JVL entry says the centre of Ashkenazi Jewry had shifted to Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia and Moravia by the early 16th century, and that after the 1648 Chmielnicki massacres Polish Jews spread westward.
A 1764 tax inquiry found that roughly seven percent of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth's population was Jewish.
Yiddish was the common language of Ashkenazi Jews in eastern and central Europe.

Sources give different shares. The JVL entry says Ashkenazim were 90% of world Jewry before the Second World War and that the Holocaust reduced their numbers; Britannica says they are more than 80% of the world's Jews today. These are estimates, and both depend on how the group is defined.
According to the JVL entry, the United States became the main centre of Ashkenazi Jewry, and in Israel and the US Ashkenazim and Sephardim live side by side, generally with separate institutions.

entries.topic: Sephardi Jews: Iberia, the 1492 expulsion, the Ottoman Empire and Judeo-Spanish

claims.text: 'Sephardim' derives from Sepharad, the Hebrew name for Spain. JVL dates Jewish life under Muslim rule in Spain from 711, a period it calls a 'Golden Age'.
In 1492 Jews in Spain who refused baptism were given four months to leave; JVL estimates that 100,000 left. In 1497 Portugal ordered its Jews out but in practice forced almost all of them to convert.

Large numbers of exiles settled in the Ottoman Empire, especially in present-day Greece and Turkey, and in North Africa; other communities formed in Venice, Livorno, Bordeaux, Bayonne, Hamburg and London.
Salonica (Thessaloniki) became a major Sephardi centre: about 35,000 Jews in the 16th century and about 80,000 around 1900, according to the University of Washington's Sephardic Studies programme.
About 50,000 Jews lived in Salonika when Germany occupied it. In 1943 the Germans deported more than 45,000 of them to Auschwitz-Birkenau, and fewer than 2,000 Jews lived in the city after the war.

Judeo-Spanish (Judezmo, also called Ladino) flourished in the Ottoman Empire after the expulsion; some scholars reserve 'Ladino' for the word-for-word liturgical translation language. The Jewish Language Project estimates about 350,000 speakers in 1900 and about 51,000 in 2024, and classes it as endangered.
JVL states that the largest Ladino-speaking community today is in Israel, with older Sephardi communities in New York, Paris, London and Latin America.

entries.topic: Western Sephardim (Spanish & Portuguese Jews): conversos, Amsterdam, London

claims.text: Historians call the communities that former Iberian 'New Christians' (conversos) built across the Dutch and English Atlantic world the 'Western Sephardim'.
After Portugal forced its Jews to convert in 1497, conversos who outwardly lived as Catholics were targets of the Inquisition, and some kept a Jewish memory for generations.

Almost a century after 1497, small groups of Portuguese New Christians began settling in Amsterdam, where they could return to Judaism openly. The Amsterdam Esnoga synagogue was inaugurated in 1675, and the community printed texts in Spanish and Portuguese.

In London, a 1656 petition to Oliver Cromwell by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel of Holland and six secret Jews led to open Jewish life in England for the first time since the 1290 expulsion. The community worshipped in a rented house in Creechurch Lane and opened Bevis Marks Synagogue in 1701, which is still in regular use.

According to the congregation's archivist, the members of London's Spanish & Portuguese congregation descended largely from Portuguese crypto-Jews. Later arrivals came from Holland, France, Italy, North Africa, Gibraltar and the Middle East.

sources.label: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization — The Making of the Western Sephardim

entries.topic: Maghrebi Jews: Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya; toshavim and megorashim

claims.text: The earliest epigraphic evidence of Jews in Morocco dates from the 2nd century CE. In 1438 the Jews of Fez were enclosed in the first Moroccan mellah (Jewish quarter).

North African sources distinguished toshavim ('residents'), the Jews already living in the Maghreb, from megorashim ('expelled'), Iberian Jews who arrived mainly after 1391 and 1492 in Fez, Tetouan, Meknes, Rabat, Salé and Marrakesh. The two groups later largely merged; in Fez a common custom was accepted only in the 18th century.
Toshavim spoke Judeo-Arabic or Judeo-Berber dialects. Megorashim brought Iberian speech, which survived in northern Morocco as the Judeo-Spanish variety Haketia.

In 1948 about 238,000 Jews lived in French Morocco, 15,000 in Spanish Morocco and 12,000 in Tangier. During Operation Yakhin (1961–64) more than 90,000 left for Israel; many others settled in France and Canada. JVL puts the Jewish population of Morocco today at about 2,100.
France's Crémieux Decree of 24 October 1870 made Algerian Jews French citizens. About 140,000 Jews lived in Algeria in 1948, and almost 130,000 moved to France after independence in 1962.

About 105,000 Jews lived in Tunisia in 1946, some 5,000 of them on the island of Djerba. Djerba's El Ghriba synagogue is traditionally called the oldest in Africa, though the present building dates from the late 19th or early 20th century.

Libya had 30,387 Jews on the eve of the Second World War. About 562 of some 2,600 Jews interned at the Giado camp died, a three-day pogrom in Tripoli in November 1945 killed 120 Jews, and 30,972 Libyan Jews later immigrated to Israel.

claims.text: The community traces its origin to the Babylonian exile under Nebuchadnezzar, with deportations from 597 BCE and the captivity conventionally dated c. 586 BCE. JVL describes it as about 2,500 years old.
The Babylonian Talmud was compiled in Babylonia, traditionally completed under Rav Ashi and Ravina; Wikipedia gives c. 520 CE for its completion.
The community spoke Baghdadi Judeo-Arabic (Judeo-Iraqi Arabic). By 1900 Baghdad's roughly 50,000 Jews were more than a quarter of the city's population.
In the Farhud pogrom in Baghdad on 1 June 1941, about 200 Jews were killed, according to Wikipedia; other counts differ.
A March 1950 Iraqi law allowed Jews to emigrate if they gave up their Iraqi citizenship. About 90,000 registered within two months, against an official expectation of no more than 8,000.

JVL says Operation Ezra and Nehemiah flew more than 120,000 Iraqi Jews to Israel, and that about 6,000 Jews remained in Iraq afterwards. Historians cited by Wikipedia estimate 120,000–130,000 people, about 75% of the community.
Today only a handful of Jews remain in Iraq. Israeli government data for 2014 counted 227,900 Jews of Iraqi descent in Israel, and broader estimates of Israelis with some Iraqi ancestry run higher.

claims.text: JVL traces the community's roots to the 6th century BCE and says that in pre-Islamic times its history was intertwined with that of neighbouring Babylon.

Judeo-Persian is the name for the literary and spoken Jewish varieties of Iranian languages, usually written in Hebrew script. The earliest known Judeo-Persian Pentateuch translation dates from 1319, and the literature flourished in the 14th–17th centuries. There was never a single spoken variety common to all Persian Jews.
By unofficial statistics 100,000–120,000 Jews lived in Iran in 1948, and about 80,000 in 1978.
Of about 60,000 Jews who left in the first ten years after the 1979 revolution, JVL says about 35,000 went to the United States (about 20,000 of them to Los Angeles) and some 20,000 to Israel.

A Jewish community remains in Iran. JVL gives undated estimates of about 8,300–9,200, and about 9,000 in a 2024 passage. A seat in parliament is reserved for a Jewish deputy; the most recent JVL lists is Siamak Moreh Sedgh (2008–2020).

claims.text: JVL dates the first evidence of Jews in Yemen to the 3rd century CE, and states that the ruling family of the Himyarite kingdom later converted to Judaism.
Yemenite Jews spoke Judeo-Yemeni Arabic, written in the Hebrew alphabet, with local varieties in Sana'a, Aden, al-Bayda and Habban. In Israel the community has largely shifted to Hebrew.
Immigration from Yemen to Ottoman Palestine began in 1882, according to JVL.
Operation Magic Carpet (also called 'On Wings of Eagles'), 1949–50, airlifted about 49,000 Jews to Israel, the vast majority from Yemen.
By 1950 almost all Yemenite Jews had moved to Israel. JVL's figures for those remaining in Yemen conflict, ranging from fewer than 50 to about 100.

claims.text: JVL cites evidence of a Jewish presence in Syria from the Seleucid period, and says the Joab ben Zeruiah synagogue in Aleppo was in use for more than 1,600 years.

The older Arabic-speaking community called itself Musta'arabim. Sephardim arrived after the 1492 expulsion and soon took a leading role; their Judeo-Syrian Arabic dialects are not known to have current speakers.
In 1947 riots in Aleppo, scores of Jews were killed and more than 200 homes, shops and synagogues destroyed. JVL gives the Jewish population of Syria in 1948 as about 40,000.
After the government formally permitted emigration in 1992, thousands left, mainly for Brooklyn and New Jersey; others settled in Israel and Mexico.

Wikipedia, citing the New York Times (2007), estimates the Brooklyn Syrian Jewish community at about 75,000, and says the largest number of Jews of Syrian descent live in Israel. JVL reports that only a handful of Jews (six, per the community head) remain in Syria.

sources.label: Jewish Virtual Library — Jews in Islamic Countries: Syria

entries.topic: Egyptian Jews: Cairo, Alexandria and the Karaites

claims.text: Jews probably settled in Fustat (Old Cairo) soon after its founding in 641. The famous Cairo Genizah was discovered in the synagogue of Ezra the Scribe, known as the Ben Ezra Synagogue.
Karaites had a large community in Fustat by the 10th century; the 1947 census counted 3,105 Karaites in Cairo.
The 1947 census counted 41,860 Jews in Cairo, 64% of Egyptian Jewry; Alexandria's community was wealthier.
Estimates of the community at its 1948 peak are 75,000 (JVL) or 75,000–80,000 (Israel's foreign ministry, cited by the University of Washington).

After the 1956 Suez–Sinai war about 25,000 Jews were expelled or forced out, many signing away their property. According to a 1957 AJC tally, the Jewish refugees who left by ship went mainly to France, Italy and Greece.
By the early 1970s nearly all had left. JVL's figures for those remaining range from a few dozen (2013) to fewer than ten (2020).

claims.text: The Encyclopaedia Judaica places Kurdistan across Turkey, Iraq and Iran, and also lists Jews in Syria. It records a tradition, noted by the 12th-century traveller Benjamin of Tudela, that Kurdistan's Jews descend from the Ten Tribes exiled by Assyria; this is a tradition, not a documented lineage.
The royal house of Adiabene in this region converted to Judaism in the mid-1st century CE. That some Kurdish Jews descend from them is presented only as a presumption.
Kurdish Jews spoke a Neo-Aramaic language with Turkish, Persian, Kurdish, Arabic and Hebrew loanwords.
There are no accurate statistics: the entry estimates 20,000–30,000 before 1948, while a 1948 Jewish Agency estimate gave about 50,000 across Iran, Iraq and Turkey.
Most Jews of Iraqi Kurdistan reached Israel via Baghdad in Operation Ezra and Nehemiah (1950–51). In Israel they live in many towns, with a large share in and around Jerusalem.

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Jewish Virtual Library — Kurdistan

claims.text: Bukhori (Bukharian, Judeo-Tajik) is a Southwestern Iranian language closely related to Tajik; the community was concentrated in Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent.
The earliest written reference is in the Talmud, which mentions a 4th-century rabbi's visit to Margiana (Merv). Jewish ossuary inscriptions from Merv date to the 5th–6th centuries.

The name comes from the Emirate of Bukhara. A Jewish quarter in the city dates from about the end of the 16th century, and in 1793 the Moroccan-born rabbi Yosef Maimon settled in Bukhara and introduced Sephardi customs.

The fall of the USSR led to mass emigration. The largest communities are now in Israel and the US; the Queens, New York community (Forest Hills, Rego Park) is estimated at 40,000–50,000, and fewer than 10,000 are thought to remain in Central Asia.
Estimates of the worldwide population differ: the Endangered Language Alliance says it 'may be as high as 200,000', while Wikipedia's infobox gives 300,000–350,000, including about 160,000 in Israel.

sources.label: Endangered Language Alliance — Bukhori
Wikipedia — Bukharan Jews (citing Moreen 2010; Encyclopaedia Judaica; Ochildiev et al. 2007)

entries.topic: Mountain Jews (Juhuro) of the eastern Caucasus

claims.text: Juhuri (Judeo-Tat) is a Southwest Iranian (Tat) language, written in semi-cursive Hebrew letters until the early Soviet period. It was spoken in towns and villages on the eastern slopes of the Caucasus.
JVL traces the community in Azerbaijan to before the 5th century, with ancestors in what is now northwestern Iran. A tradition of descent from the Lost Tribes is reported but not established.
Quba's Jewish settlement was established in 1742 by Fatali Khan as a refuge for Jews; the Soviets renamed it Krasnaya Sloboda ('Red Settlement').
Azerbaijan's Jewish community numbered about 80,000 in the early 1990s. Emigration to Israel, Russia and Germany then reduced it sharply; JVL gives about 30,000 Jews of all backgrounds in 2016.
Juhuri speakers now live mainly in Israel and the US (centred in Flatbush, Brooklyn), and thousands remain in Dagestan and Azerbaijan. The worldwide population is estimated at 100,000–200,000.

sources.label: Endangered Language Alliance — Juhuri
Jewish Virtual Library (Joanna Sloame) — Azerbaijan Virtual Jewish History Tour

claims.text: The most widely held tradition in Georgia says Jews first arrived after Nebuchadnezzar's conquest of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. The 11th-century chronicler Leonti Mroveli gives a similar account, but the dating rests on tradition and chronicle, not contemporary records.
There is no documentation of the language Jews spoke when they arrived. Their speech is described as a Jewish variety of Georgian (Judeo-Georgian, also called Kivruli or Gruzinic).
In 1939 Jews were 1.1% of Georgia's population. Many emigrated to Israel in the 1970s wave, and in the 1990s most of the rest left for Israel, Russia, Europe and America.
Wikipedia gives conflicting figures of 65,000 and about 75,000 for Georgian Jews in Israel, and about 1,500 remaining in Georgia as of 2014.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Georgian Jews (citing Lerner 2004 and others)
Jewish Language Project, HUC (T. Lomtadze & R. Enoch) — Judeo-Georgian

claims.text: The Romaniotes are Greek Jews documented since the Byzantine period. Their ancestors were settled in the eastern Roman world long before the empire divided.

Their language, Yevanic (Judaeo-Greek), was written in Hebrew letters until the 19th century and was mutually intelligible with local Greek. As late as the early 20th century, Jews in Ioannina, Arta, Preveza and Chalkida still spoke a distinct Jewish Greek.
Yevanic declined mainly as Romaniotes were absorbed into the Ladino-speaking Sephardi communities that grew in Greece after the late 15th century.
The Holocaust nearly destroyed the language. Today small numbers of Romaniotes live in Greece (including a few elderly speakers in Ioannina as of 2019), Israel and the United States.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Yevanic (citing Spolsky & Benor 2006; Dalven 1971; Ethnologue)

entries.topic: Italian Jews (Italkim) and the Jews of Rome

claims.text: JVL dates Rome's Jewish community to 161 BCE, when envoys of Judah Maccabee arrived, and calls it the oldest Jewish community in Europe.
The Jewish Language Project says Jews have lived in the Italian peninsula perhaps since the 2nd century BCE, and that the earliest settlers were probably Greek-speaking.
Italian Jews kept their own prayer rite, the Nusach Italki.
Judeo-Italian is a group of varieties: literary texts in Hebrew script survive mostly from 1200–1700. Judeo-Roman is perhaps the only variety still spoken, by a small, mostly elderly group.
In 1555 Pope Paul IV ordered the Jews confined to ghettos. On 16 October 1943 the Nazis deported Rome's Jews to Auschwitz, and only a dozen of those deported survived.
About 15,000 Jews live in Rome today, according to JVL.

sources.label: Jewish Virtual Library — Virtual Jewish World: Rome, Italy
Jewish Language Project, HUC (Aaron Rubin) — Judeo-Italian

claims.text: 'Beta Israel' means 'House of Israel'; the outside name falasha is described as derogatory, meaning 'outsider'. The community called the Torah 'Orit'.

Their origin is disputed. The Beta Israel themselves held a tradition of descent from the tribe of Dan, probably linked to the 9th-century Eldad ha-Dani story; they reject the Menelik/Queen of Sheba legend. A modern theory links them to Agaw groups who adopted Judaism from South Arabian Jews.

Historian Steven Kaplan (1992) argues they are not a lost tribe but an ethnic group that emerged in Ethiopia between the 14th and 16th centuries. My Jewish Learning instead suggests they arrived between the 1st and 6th centuries. There is no consensus.
Their holy books and prayers are in Ge'ez, a liturgical language also used by Ethiopian Christians. Most spoke Amharic, and those from the Tigray region spoke Tigrinya.
On 9 February 1973 Sephardi Chief Rabbi Ovadia Yosef ruled that they are Jews, and in 1975 an Israeli interministerial commission recognised them under the Law of Return.

Operation Moses (1984–85) airlifted 7,700 Jews from refugee camps in Sudan, and Operation Solomon (1991) brought 14,400 from Ethiopia, according to Shalvah Weil. Figures for Operation Moses vary between sources.
Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics put the Jewish population of Ethiopian origin in Israel at 177,600 in 2024 (as reported by JNS).

claims.text: Britannica calls the Bene Israel the largest and oldest of India's Jewish groups. By their tradition they descend from survivors of a shipwreck on the Konkan coast more than 2,100 years ago; the EJ notes that other origin theories (Yemeni, Babylonian-Persian) were proposed later.
They lived for centuries in Konkan villages with Marathi as their mother tongue, and neighbours called them Shanivar Teli ('Sabbath-observing oil-pressers').
From the mid-18th century many moved to Bombay. The first Bene Israel synagogue, Sha'ar ha-Rachamim, was founded there in 1796 by army officer Samuel Ezekiel Divekar.
In 1962 Israel's Chief Rabbinate council allowed marriage with Bene Israel subject to genealogical checks. After protests in 1964, the government declared them 'Jews in every respect'.
More than 12,000 Bene Israel emigrated to Israel between 1948 and 1969. The EJ entry gives about 80,000 in Israel today and about 4,000 in India in the early 21st century.

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bene Israel (summary only)
Encyclopaedia Judaica (2nd ed.) via Jewish Virtual Library — Bene Israel

claims.text: The oldest documentary evidence of Jews in Kerala is a set of copper plates of about 1000 CE, granting privileges to Joseph Rabban from the ruler of Cranganore (which Jews called Shingly). Community tradition and the Jewish Language Project place Jews in Kerala much earlier, 'since at least the beginning of the common era'.
A flood in 1341 silted up Cranganore and opened Cochin's harbour, and Jews moved south. In 1568 the Paradesi ('foreign') Jews built their synagogue beside the Maharaja's palace in Cochin.
Western writers labelled Paradesis 'white Jews' and the older Malabari communities 'black Jews', but My Jewish Learning notes skin colour did not always match the distinction.
Kerala's Jews spoke Jewish Malayalam, a Malayalam variety with Hebrew loanwords. About 2,500 speakers lived in India in the 1940s; the Jewish Language Project estimates about 100 speakers in 2024.
Most emigrated to Israel after 1948, with the largest number arriving in 1954. My Jewish Learning estimates well over 4,000 Cochinim in Israel and about 60 Jews remaining in Kerala.

sources.label: My Jewish Learning (Barbara C. Johnson, via The Israel Museum) — The Cochin Jews of Kerala

claims.text: Arabic-speaking Jewish merchants from Aleppo, Baghdad and Basra first settled in the port of Surat; close to 100 were there by the end of the 18th century.
Many Iraqi Jews arrived in the early 19th century, fleeing the rule of Daud Pasha (1817–31). David Sassoon arrived in Bombay in 1833.
Calcutta's Baghdadi community exceeded 1,800 by the end of the 19th century; the whole community never exceeded about 5,000.
Most Baghdadis switched directly from Arabic to English.
After Indian independence most left, the wealthier for England, Canada, the US and Australia, and a relatively small share for Israel. Barely 200 remained in the mid-1990s.

sources.label: My Jewish Learning (Joan G. Roland) — The Baghdadi Jews of India

claims.text: Encyclopaedia Iranica says most scholars agree the Kaifeng Jews came from Persia in the 12th century, under the Song dynasty; Wikipedia summarises scholarly consensus as primarily Persian Jewish origin.

The dating is disputed. Some scholars place arrival in the Tang dynasty or earlier, while most favour the Song period. The synagogue is traditionally dated to 1163, but Peng Yu (2017) argues the names linked to that date were back-dated.
The community's earliest stele, dated 1489, says the Jews came from Tianzhu (India). Some rubrics in their prayer books are in Judeo-Persian.
In 1605 Ai Tian, a member of the community, met the Jesuit Matteo Ricci in Beijing.
A flood in 1642 destroyed the synagogue. It was dismantled sometime between 1850 and 1866, and by the 19th century the community's Jewish practice had largely ended.

Estimates of descendants today range from about 500 to 1,000, of whom 40–50 take part in Jewish activities. Israel does not recognise them as Jews by birth and requires conversion; 19 emigrated with Shavei Israel's help between 2006 and 2016.

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Donald D. Leslie) — Kaifeng
Wikipedia — Kaifeng Jews (citing Sharot 2007; Eber 1993; Yu 2017; Leslie 2008)

entries.topic: Karaites (a stream of Judaism): Iraq, Egypt, Crimea, Lithuania

claims.text: Karaism relies on the Hebrew Bible alone and rejects the Oral Law (Mishnah and Talmud) as binding.

The movement grew from the followers of Anan ben David, who about 760 CE was passed over for the office of exilarch in Babylonia. His followers were first called Ananites; the name Karaites appears later.
Karaites had a large community in Fustat (Old Cairo) by the 10th century; Cairo still had 3,105 Karaites in 1947.
The Crimean Karaites (Karaim) speak a Kipchak Turkic language. Their tradition says Grand Duke Vytautas moved a branch to Lithuania (Trakai), but the date of that move is disputed.

In the Russian Empire, Crimean Karaites won exemption from anti-Jewish laws, gaining the same rights as their Christian and Tatar neighbours in 1863. Under hakham Seraya Shapshal (elected 1928) a doctrine of non-Jewish, Khazar descent developed, and a 1939 Nazi genealogical office ruling said Karaites were not a Jewish religious community.

Whether the Crimean Karaim are Jewish by descent is disputed. Many reject a Semitic origin and identify as Khazar descendants, while genetic studies (Brook 2014) find partial Middle Eastern ancestry close to other Jewish groups, and Israel's Chief Rabbinate treats Karaites as Jews.
The New World Encyclopedia puts the Karaites in Israel at about 12,000, mostly near Ramla, and says most of its Board of Hakhams are of Egyptian descent.

claims.text: The Abayudaya began practising Judaism in 1919, after the Ugandan leader Semei Kakungulu declared himself a Jew.
Since 2002 conversions in the community have been overseen by the Conservative movement.

The Jewish Agency has recognised the Abayudaya as Jewish, but Israel's Interior Ministry rejected an Abayudaya member's citizenship application and set a policy that 'emerging' communities are not eligible under the Law of Return.
The community is a 20th-century religious movement; it does not claim continuous descent from ancient Israel in the sources consulted.

sources.label: Intermountain Jewish News (4 Feb 2021) — Abayudaya may not come on aliyah

entries.topic: Bnei Menashe (northeast India): claimed descent, disputed

claims.text: The Bnei Menashe of Mizoram and Manipur say they descend from the biblical tribe of Manasseh.
In 2005 Sephardi Chief Rabbi Shlomo Amar recognised them as descendants of a lost tribe, but rabbinical judges required formal conversion to Orthodox Judaism before emigration.

The descent claim is not established. A 2003 Technion test was never formally published, and a 2004 Kolkata study, which was not peer-reviewed, found no clear evidence of Middle Eastern origin among men.
About 3,500 had moved to Israel by 2019. In late November 2025 Israel approved bringing the remaining roughly 5,800 over five years, mainly to the Galilee.

sources.label: Al Jazeera (6 Apr 2005) — Indian 'lost tribe' set to move to Israel
EastMojo (20 Jan 2026) — How faith, history and politics shaped Mizoram's Bnei Menashe identity

claims.text: The Lemba live in small groups in northeastern South Africa and in central and eastern Zimbabwe. Their oral tradition places their origin in 'Sena'.
For much of the 20th century some Lemba have claimed Jewish or Semitic ancestry; most Lemba today are Christian.

A 1996 study by Trefor Jenkins reported half of sampled Lemba Y chromosomes as 'Semitic' in origin. Parfitt and colleagues (2000) found the 'Cohen Modal Haplotype' in over half of one sub-clan, which the EJ says can be read 'with great caution'.
A 2014 reassessment by Tofanelli and colleagues concluded that such haplotype motifs are not reliable predictors of Jewish ancestry, which weakens genetic arguments of this kind.

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Judaica (2nd ed., Tudor Parfitt) via Encyclopedia.com — Lemba
